In the case of the vowels they're diphthongs and triphthongs. English doesn't have a lot of those because the same vowels are reused for different sounds in different contexts (like o is "ih" in women but "awe" in organisation.

In Irish vowels are always pronounced the same in every word, but sometimes they're combined together to make new sounds. Kinda like how æ used to fall between a and e in English. Historically English was much more like that but with early modern english they dropped phonetic spelling and went nuts.

The consonants are a bit more confusing because they get more heavily modified. Basically like many other european languages we dropped our case endings to make the language simpler, but as a result other parts of pronunciation had to carry that meaning. In the case of Irish it's often by modifying consonants.

So "an fear" ("on far," the man) becomes "an fhear" ("on arr, belonging to the man) in the genative case. Irish speakers understand that transition intuitively and it's a solid rule with no exceptions, but to a non Irish speaker that is incomprehensible.

Celtic languages are broadly split into two groups: P-celtic and Q-celtic, so named because of a consonant shift that occurred back in the bronze age at some point. words that have a k/c/q sound in Q-celtic languages have a p sound in P-celtic. So "Mac" (mack, son, Irish) becomes "Ap" (app, son, Welsh). "Ceann" (kyoun, head, Irish) becomes "Pen" (pen, head, Welsh) and so on.

Historically most celtic languages were P-celtic and were spoken across Europe (Britain, Iberia, France, the Benelux Region, Northern Italy, The Alps, possibly bits of Northern Germany, The Balkans Romania and Northern Turkey). They were broadly mutually intelligable and somewhat mutually intelligable with the Italic languages. Q-celtic was spoken in Ireland and Irish colonies.

Depending on who you listen to the language either evolved in Ireland, spread across Europe and mutated into P-celtic, or it originated in Austria and spread out radially, mutating into Q-celtic when it hit Ireland.
